slides.title: Business Processes Impacting Security Operation
points: Change management helps organizations make changes in a controlled, documented, and reversible way.
Objective 1.3 focuses on the business processes that reduce security and operational risk during change.

slides.title: Change Management
slides.teach: Change management is the controlled process for planning, reviewing, approving, testing, implementing, documenting, and—when necessary—reversing changes.

course.learn: Change management is the controlled process for planning, reviewing, approving, testing, implementing, documenting, and—when necessary—reversing changes.

breakdown.explanation: Instead of changing production systems whenever someone wants, the organization uses a defined process so changes are understood, authorized, tested, and traceable.
Software updates, firewall-rule changes, server migrations, configuration changes, network upgrades.

course.why: Poorly controlled changes can introduce vulnerabilities, cause outages, break dependencies, or make incident response harder because nobody knows exactly what changed.
course.example: A network administrator needs to modify production firewall rules. The change is reviewed, approved, tested, scheduled, documented, and given a backout plan before deployment.
course.exam: If a scenario emphasizes approval, impact analysis, test results, a maintenance window, ownership, stakeholders, documentation, or a backout plan, think CHANGE MANAGEMENT.
course.check_q: Why is change management important to security?
course.check_a: It reduces the risk that changes introduce vulnerabilities, outages, undocumented configurations, or other unintended consequences.

slides.title: Approval Process
slides.teach: The approval process requires an authorized person or group to review and approve a proposed change before implementation.

course.learn: The approval process requires an authorized person or group to review and approve a proposed change before implementation.

breakdown.explanation: Someone with the proper authority gives permission before the change reaches production.
Change Advisory Board approval, manager approval, security review, formal change ticket approval.

course.why: Approval prevents unauthorized or poorly evaluated changes from being introduced into the environment.
course.example: An engineer prepares a production firewall change, but cannot deploy it until the designated change authority approves the request.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'Who gives permission before the change?' → APPROVAL PROCESS.
course.check_q: A production change cannot be deployed until a manager signs off on the request. Which process is being used?

slides.title: Ownership
slides.teach: Ownership identifies the person or team responsible for the change from planning through completion.

course.learn: Ownership identifies the person or team responsible for the change from planning through completion.

breakdown.explanation: There should be a clearly accountable owner who coordinates the work and makes sure the change is completed correctly.
Change owner, application owner, service owner, implementation owner.

course.why: Without clear ownership, tasks can be missed, communication can fail, and nobody may be accountable when a change causes a problem.
course.example: A database upgrade has one engineer assigned as the change owner who coordinates testing, deployment, validation, and rollback if needed.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'Who is responsible for the change?' → OWNERSHIP.
course.check_q: Which change-management concept identifies who is accountable for coordinating a change?

slides.title: Stakeholders
slides.teach: Stakeholders are people or groups who are affected by, depend on, approve, support, or have an interest in the change.

course.learn: Stakeholders are people or groups who are affected by, depend on, approve, support, or have an interest in the change.

breakdown.explanation: Before making the change, identify who could be impacted and who needs to know about it.
Users, application owners, security teams, help desk, business managers, vendors, compliance teams.

course.why: Stakeholder communication reduces surprises and ensures important business or technical impacts are considered before implementation.
course.example: A payroll-system upgrade may affect HR, finance, IT support, security, and employees who use payroll services.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'Who is affected or needs to be informed?' → STAKEHOLDERS.
course.check_q: A planned server change may affect HR, finance, and the help desk. What should the change team identify?

slides.title: Impact Analysis
slides.teach: Impact analysis evaluates how a proposed change could affect systems, users, security controls, dependencies, availability, and business operations.

course.learn: Impact analysis evaluates how a proposed change could affect systems, users, security controls, dependencies, availability, and business operations.

breakdown.explanation: Ask what could break, who could be affected, and what new risks the change could introduce.
Dependency review, security-impact review, outage analysis, compatibility assessment, business-impact evaluation.

course.why: A change that looks safe on one system may disrupt another service, weaken a control, or create downtime elsewhere.
course.example: Before disabling an old protocol, the team checks which applications still depend on it and what business services could fail.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'What could this change affect or break?' → IMPACT ANALYSIS.
course.check_q: Which process would most likely identify that a firewall-rule change could break payroll connectivity?

slides.title: Test Results
slides.teach: Test results provide evidence that a proposed change was tested and behaved as expected before or during deployment.

course.learn: Test results provide evidence that a proposed change was tested and behaved as expected before or during deployment.

breakdown.explanation: Testing shows whether the change works safely before it is trusted in production.
Lab test results, staging-environment results, validation checks, security testing, regression testing.

course.why: Testing helps identify failures, compatibility problems, and security issues before users or production systems are affected.
course.example: A software patch is installed in a staging environment and tested for application compatibility before production deployment.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'Did the change work safely in testing?' → TEST RESULTS.
course.check_q: A team reviews evidence from a staging environment before approving a production patch. What are they reviewing?

slides.title: Backout Plan
slides.teach: A backout plan contains the documented steps needed to reverse a failed change and restore the previous known-good state.

course.learn: A backout plan contains the documented steps needed to reverse a failed change and restore the previous known-good state.

breakdown.explanation: It is the 'undo plan' prepared before the change is deployed.
Restore previous configuration, uninstall an update, revert a virtual-machine snapshot, reinstall the previous software version.

course.why: Changes can fail even after testing. A backout plan reduces recovery time and limits downtime when implementation goes wrong.
course.example: A new network configuration causes an outage, so the administrator follows the prewritten steps to restore the old configuration.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'How do we undo the change?' → BACKOUT PLAN.
course.check_q: A production update causes a failure and the team follows documented steps to restore the previous version. What are they using?

slides.title: Maintenance Window
slides.teach: A maintenance window is an approved period when potentially disruptive changes can be performed.

course.learn: A maintenance window is an approved period when potentially disruptive changes can be performed.

breakdown.explanation: The organization schedules risky or outage-producing work for a time when the business impact will be lower.
Sunday 2:00–4:00 AM maintenance, scheduled patching period, planned network outage window.

course.why: Scheduling changes helps control downtime, coordinate support staff, and communicate expected service interruptions.
course.example: A database upgrade that requires two hours of downtime is scheduled for early Sunday morning when usage is lowest.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'When are we allowed to perform the change?' → MAINTENANCE WINDOW.
course.check_q: A company waits until 2:00 AM Sunday to perform a change that may interrupt service. What concept is this?

slides.title: Standard Operating Procedure
slides.teach: A standard operating procedure (SOP) is documented, repeatable guidance for performing a routine task consistently.

course.learn: A standard operating procedure (SOP) is documented, repeatable guidance for performing a routine task consistently.

breakdown.explanation: It describes the approved normal way to perform an operation.
Patch-deployment procedure, account-provisioning procedure, backup procedure, server-build checklist.

course.why: SOPs reduce inconsistency, help staff follow approved practices, and make recurring work easier to train, audit, and repeat.
course.example: Every monthly patch cycle follows the same documented sequence for testing, approval, deployment, verification, and documentation.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'How do we normally perform this repeatable task?' → STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE.
course.check_q: Which document describes the approved repeatable steps for a routine operational task?

blocks.title: Change management exam shortcuts
rows: Who is affected or needs to know?
What could break or be affected?
Did it work safely in testing?
How do we undo the change?
When can we perform disruptive work?
How do we normally perform this task?

blocks.title: Read the scenario and ask what part of the change process is missing
items: If the question asks who must authorize the change before implementation, think approval process.
Example: A firewall rule cannot be deployed until the change board signs off.
If the question asks who is accountable for coordinating the change, think ownership.
Example: One engineer is assigned to oversee testing, deployment, and rollback.
If the question asks about downstream effects, dependencies, outages, or security risks, think impact analysis.
Example: The team checks whether disabling TLS 1.0 will break an older application.
If the question asks how to restore the previous known-good state after failure, think backout plan.
Example: A failed update is reversed using documented rollback steps.
When can we do it? → Maintenance Window
If a disruptive change is scheduled for a low-impact approved time, think maintenance window.
Example: A network upgrade is scheduled for Sunday at 2:00 AM.
If the task is routine and follows the same documented steps each time, think standard operating procedure.
Example: Monthly patching follows an approved checklist.
blocks.example: Fast memory: Permission · Owner · Affected people · Impact · Test · Undo · Time · Repeatable procedure

questions.q: A firewall change must be reviewed and formally authorized before it can be deployed to production. Which change-management process is being used?
questions.explanation: The approval process provides authorized permission before implementation.

questions.q: A database upgrade has one engineer responsible for coordinating testing, deployment, validation, and rollback. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Ownership identifies the person or team accountable for the change.

questions.q: Before a payroll upgrade, the team identifies HR, finance, the help desk, and security as groups that may be affected. What is the team identifying?
questions.explanation: Stakeholders are people or groups affected by or interested in the change.

questions.q: A team checks whether disabling an old protocol will break any applications that still depend on it. Which change-management activity is this?
questions.explanation: Impact analysis evaluates what a proposed change could affect or break.

questions.q: A patch is installed in staging and validated before production deployment. What artifact helps demonstrate that the patch behaved as expected?
questions.explanation: Test results provide evidence about how the change behaved during testing.

questions.q: A software update causes a production failure, so the team restores the previous known-good version using prewritten steps. What are they using?
questions.explanation: A backout plan defines how to reverse a failed change.

questions.q: A disruptive upgrade is scheduled for Sunday at 2:00 AM when business activity is lowest. Which concept is this?
questions.explanation: A maintenance window is an approved period for potentially disruptive work.

questions.q: Every monthly patch cycle follows the same approved, documented sequence. What best describes that document?
questions.explanation: An SOP defines repeatable instructions for a routine process.
